articles.title: Elderly Palestinian woman killed, 19 wounded by Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Monday, November 16, marked another horrific night for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank after illegal Israeli settlers launched simultaneous assaults against civilians in the eastern governorate of Jericho, and the southern governorate of Bethlehem. Israeli settlers opened fire on Palestinian residents in Ad-Duyuk at-Tahta village west of Jericho, killing 72-year-old woman Fadda Fheidat and injuring 10 others. A relative of Fheidat told Palestine News and Information Agency WAFA , that the Israeli forces prohibited the family from holding a funeral procession in the village on Tuesday, November 17. Israeli soldiers also beat a Palestinian photographer working for the same news agency on Tuesday morning while he was covering the events in the village. The photographer sustained fractures and bruises and was transferred to a hospital to receive medical treatment. The deadly assault on Ad-Duyuk at-Tahta came two weeks after Israeli settlers – backed by the right-wing settlement organization Nachala – seized several Palestinian homes in the village, displacing dozens of residents. Meanwhile, eight Palestinians were injured in the town of Tuqu’, south of Bethlehem, late Monday after an Israeli settler rammed them with his vehicle. According to a recent report released by the United Nations, over 1,122 Palestinians, including 246 children, were killed in attacks carried out by Israeli forces and illegal colonists in the occupied West Bank between October 7, 2023, and July 24, 2026.

articles.title: The US and Israel are inventing excuses for fresh escalation, says Iran
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Iran has rejected reports about its possible involvement in planned attacks inside US cities, claiming them to be a part of a malicious campaign against the country waged to justify a possible new escalation in the US-Israeli war. “From the so-called ‘refrigerator cases’ in France to allegations that Iran is plotting to assassinate US officials, we are witnessing what appears to be a coordinated malign narrative campaign,” Esmail Baghaei, official spokesperson of Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, pointed out in a post on X on Monday, November 16. After several supermarkets in France reported their fridges heating abnormally in October, its government claimed it was a result of a cyberattack and accused Iran for the same. Iran had vehemently denied the allegations , calling them baseless and absurd. Despite Iranian denials, France is now seeking fresh EU sanctions against Iran over the issue. The purpose behind such a campaign “is to portray Iran not merely as a threat to Western governments, but as an enemy of ordinary people and their everyday lives,” Baghaei argued. Baghaei’s comments were referring to a CNN report on Monday which claimed that Iran was involved in a plan to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington targeting senior US officials. The report quotes seven US officials as a source for the story without giving any names. The White House, in a statement on Monday, however, has denied any such threats. Last week, several reports indicated that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was relocated into a military base after facing threats to his life from Iran, without providing any evidence or sources of the information. There were also rumors about several US officials, including President Donald Trump, taking shelter in bunkers due to the Iranian threats. Attempts to seek justification for fresh escalation Arguing that such reports regarding the possible Iranian involvement in bombing and murder plots is nothing but attempts to manufacture fear for public support to continue the war on Iran “and to legitimize their leaders’ reckless political and military actions under the pretext of protecting public safety,” Baghaei added. Iran has not done anything to harm common civilians of aggressor states so far despite intense provocations and targeting against its own civilians and political leadership and do not intend to do so in future as well, Baghaei said. Scores of Iran’s political and military leaders including the Supreme Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Khamenei and hundreds of civilians, including over 160 school children in Minab were killed during US-Israeli attacks. Baghaei warned against the deliberate misreporting and manipulation by the media, claiming “Iran does not need to become a mirror image of its wicked aggressors to defeat them.” In a similar instance, speaker of the Iranian Parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf criticized a report in The New York Times on Tuesday, claiming it was an attempt to seek justification for fresh attacks on Iran’s dams and other water sources. The New York Times published the report on Monday, with reporters claiming Iran deliberately built dams near its missile and military sites, alluding they were for dual use. Ghalibaf questioned the credentials of the so-called experts behind the report claiming the story was possibly planted to justify attacks on civilian infrastructure in the country and warned that any such move will invite similar Iranian retaliation to dams or power plants located near the US military bases. Several other commentators have called The New York Times report a “disgrace to journalism,” claiming it amounts to complicity in war crimes. President Trump has repeatedly threatened to attack Iran’s civilian and economic infrastructure during the war which began in February. After facing defeat in the midterm elections earlier this month, he has moderated his rhetoric about launching fresh strikes escalating the war and even claimed the war may end soon. However, the fresh US deployment of troops and warships in West Asia continues. On Monday, the US deployed USS Theodore Roosvelt, taking the number of such warships deployed in the region to three.

articles.title: Killing of activist Vigário Luís Balanta officially under investigation
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The government of Guinea-Bissau has established a commission of inquiry to investigate the assassination of political activist Vigário Luís Balanta, nearly eight months after his killing. Balanta, leader of the Pó di Terra Revolutionary Movement, was found dead on March 31, 2026, on the outskirts of Bolanhas de N’Dam, approximately 30 kilometers from the capital, Bissau. His body was found with visible injuries, torn clothing and other signs of violence, raising suspicions that he had been tortured before being killed. Read more: Political activist in Guinea-Bissau found beaten to death Speaking to BreakThrough News , Janó Embana, coordinator of the Association of Revolutionary Pan-Africanist Youth of Guinea-Bissau (AJOPAR), welcomed the announcement of an investigation by the Office of the Attorney-General on November 9, 2026, while questioning why authorities had taken so long to act. “The decision deserves to be welcomed. However, we cannot ignore the long period of institutional silence that preceded it, nor the political and security circumstances which, in my view, help explain why it took so long for an investigation of this nature to be formally established,” Embana said. He argued that the absence of a formal investigation and publicly presented findings for several months had raised questions about the independence of state institutions and possible political interference in the administration of justice. Adding, the inquiry must go beyond identifying those who directly carried out the killing. He insisted that investigators should also go after the alleged masterminds, financiers, facilitators, and anyone involved in concealing the crime. “The establishment of a commission does not, in itself, mean that justice has been achieved. Our expectation is that the investigation will be transparent, credible, independent and conducted rigorously, without political or military interference,” he said. He further warned against the investigation being used to rehabilitate the image of political figures or institutions seeking to benefit from the country’s changing political circumstances “We do not want selective justice, guided by the convenience of those in power. We want justice that reaches everyone responsible, regardless of their political, military or institutional position,” Embana said. Read more: Guinea-Bissau: A coup staged to protect the neocolonial order? Since the November 2025 military takeover, Guinea-Bissau’s political conditions have changed with growing repression, intimidation and restrictions on opposition forces and dissenting voices. The military intervention, which followed a disputed electoral process widely viewed by critics as an attempt to prevent the PAIGC-led coalition from taking power, ushered in a new period of political uncertainty and heightened tensions. Read more: Military government in Guinea-Bissau seeks to reshape political system with referendum As the demand for accountability continues, Embana described Balanta’s killing as a major loss for Guinea-Bissau’s political and social struggles, remembering him as part of a generation of young activists seeking to challenge injustice and transform the country’s political and social conditions. Balanta’s involvement in the Pó di Terra movement, he said, reflected his commitment to political resistance and social transformation. “Vigário Luís Balanta was our brother, comrade and activist. He represented a generation of young people who refused to passively accept injustice,” Embana said. He added that “Justice for Vigário Luís Balanta is not merely a demand of his family or comrades. It is a demand of an entire society that can no longer continue to coexist with impunity.”

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands reject Czech government’s media reform plans
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Prague on Sunday, November 15, to protest against the Czech government’s plans to reform the financing model of public service media . The administration led by Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pushed to replace the current license fee model for Czech Television and Czech Radio with direct financing from the state budget – a change critics fear would make the broadcasters more vulnerable to government pressure. Read more: In defense of press freedom, we demand an end to Israel’s genocide In addition to that, the reform would cut the broadcasters’ funding by approximately 15%, which casts additional doubts about the final impacts on program production. “Such a funding model opens the door to political pressure and threatens editorial independence,” warned the European Federation of Journalists (EFJ) and other associations at the beginning of November. “When public service media depend on annual budget decisions made by those in power, there is a serious risk that funding will become a tool for influencing journalism and editorial decisions.” The proposal is being rushed through legislative procedure, including through an overnight vote in late October, prompting widespread outrage. This, in turn, led to several mobilizations and a one-day strike by Czech Television and Czech Radio workers at the beginning of November. Protesters critical of public service media programming The demonstrations are continuing despite viewers’ own frustrations with the broadcasters’ performance. Yet most protesters appear to have concluded that the government’s path will not change this for the better. Instead, they warn that the cuts would most likely affect the parts of programming that still offer a glimpse of critical thought or formation. “We understand that for many, the long-standing political bias in the news coverage and on-air conduct of some Czech Television employees is a reason to hesitate in supporting this institution,” the progressive party Strana Levice wrote ahead of the November strike. “We too oppose the deeply ingrained anti-left sentiment, the contempt for unions and social movements, and the blind repetition of Israeli propaganda.” “The actions of the Babiš government will not improve their work,” they added. “Quite the opposite. Nothing will change in the areas that part of the public rightly criticizes. However, there will be cuts to cultural and dramatic production, the production of minority genre programs, and so on. The same applies to Czech Radio, whose unique sound archive could easily fall victim to privatization.” Media associations across Europe call for rebuilding public service media The scale of the mobilization in Prague has been recognized as an important moment region-wide, given parallel efforts to weaken public service media across Europe. Source: AP News “What matters is how the people in Prague took to the streets to defend their public media – not because they’re perfect, but because they know how important they are,” Maja Sever , EFJ president, wrote after participating in the protest. “As always, I’m super optimistic in believing that this could be something much bigger than the courage and determination of our friends in the Czech Republic,” she wrote. “That the energy of hundreds of thousands of people who took to the streets to defend Czech Television and Czech Radio could become part of a broader European story about defending public service media.”

articles.title: He resisted Israeli occupation in Palestine. Italy is imprisoning him for it.
articles.author: Dario Morgante
articles.content: Italy jailed a Palestinian activist as a terrorist for resisting Israeli occupation in the West Bank. His case tests the limits of international law and the reach of the Israeli regime.

articles.title: The victory of student populism
articles.author: Srđan Atanasovski
articles.content: T he victory of the Student List in Serbia’s parliamentary elections on October 25, 2026 marks the end of fourteen years of domination by Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party. With approximately 53 percent of the vote and a projected absolute majority in parliament, the Student List achieved a result that until recently had seemed almost unimaginable. The nature of this victory, and Serbia’s political future, are difficult to understand through the conventional categories of government versus opposition, liberalism versus conservatism, or European integration versus national sovereignty. At the center of Serbia’s political transformation was a mass student movement, while behind it lay a conflict between two elites: the political elite built by Vučić’s regime over the previous decade and a half, and an academic elite that had remained relatively independent of his system of rule. The decisive factor was the latter’s ability to forge an alliance with the student movement, which had developed a distinctive form of participatory populism. This alliance made possible the political mobilisation that brought about the change of government. This populist movement did not emerge around demands for a radical transformation of Serbia’s economic or foreign policy. In many areas, it reproduced the existing political consensus, promising that similar policies could be pursued without corruption, organized crime, nepotism, and party based employment. The greatest challenge facing the new government will be to dismantle the previous regime’s clientelist mechanisms while demonstrating whether its relatively popular economic model can be maintained without relying on the same mechanisms of capital accumulation and political control. A one-party system within a multiparty democracy One of the most important features of Vučić’s political domination was the systematic weakening of the multiparty system, even as the formal institutions of parliamentary democracy remained in place. The Serbian Progressive Party sought to incorporate almost every political actor with significant electoral support. Political organizations and their leaders were offered positions within the governing coalition, often through guaranteed places on joint electoral lists, while those who refused to cooperate faced various forms of pressure, marginalisation, and political destruction. The result was an attempt to establish a kind of one-party system within a formally multiparty democracy. Almost every significant ideological position could be found within the governing coalition, from nationalist and conservative to liberal, pro-European, and socially oriented currents. Ideological conflicts were largely transferred from electoral competition to the internal relations of the governing bloc. Elections increasingly became referendums on the exercise of power and attitudes towards Vučić’s regime rather than contests between alternative political programs. Opposition parties that remained outside this system failed to build a sufficiently broad social base or establish a different political agenda. Vučić developed an exceptionally extensive party and electoral machine…Membership in the ruling party, or a willingness to secure votes for it, became an important prerequisite for employment, career advancement, and access to public resources. Gradually, this system extended beyond its electoral function and became a fundamental mechanism for organizing social and economic relations. At the same time, Vučić developed an exceptionally extensive party and electoral machine. Its operation depended on political loyalty, control over public-sector employment, the collection of so-called capillary votes, and various forms of pressure on voters. Membership in the ruling party, or a willingness to secure votes for it, became an important prerequisite for employment, career advancement, and access to public resources. Gradually, this system extended beyond its electoral function and became a fundamental mechanism for organizing social and economic relations. For a teacher who had spent years on temporary contracts, a healthcare worker waiting for permanent employment, or an employee of a public enterprise, party affiliation could directly determine their professional future. Similar mechanisms spread into the private sector through networks of business connections, public procurement, and privileged access to state resources. Alongside the major financial scandals reported in the media, corruption became an everyday experience for a large part of the population. Almost anyone seeking employment, career advancement, or access to a particular entitlement could encounter the consequences of party clientelism. Alongside systemic nepotism, the regime was marred by serious scandals that raised questions about links between state structures and organized crime. These included the Jovanjica case, involving the discovery of a large marijuana plantation allegedly protected by members of the security services, and a murder in a Belgrade restaurant, whose alleged cover- up implicated the then-head of the Belgrade police. The problem for Vučić was that, once established, the network of loyalty required the continuous protection of its members. Sanctioning individuals for criminal activity or corruption could threaten the stability of the entire system, which rested on the expectation that political loyalty would be rewarded and protected. The electoral machine thus gradually became a burden on the regime itself. The mechanisms that enabled it to remain in power simultaneously generated increasingly widespread social discontent. The problem for Vučić was that, once established, the network of loyalty required the continuous protection of its members. Sanctioning individuals for criminal activity or corruption could threaten the stability of the entire system…The electoral machine thus gradually became a burden on the regime itself. The academic elite Vučić failed to incorporate Unlike the political and business elites, which he successfully connected through a system of mutual interests, Vučić never managed to fully incorporate Serbia’s academic elite. By academic elite, I mean a broader stratum of highly educated professionals, professional managers, economists, lawyers, intellectuals, university professors, researchers, and people working in non-governmental organisations. Their social authority rests primarily on education, professional qualifications, and experience rather than control over the party apparatus. Throughout his rule, Vučić attempted to win over sections of this elite. Ana Brnabić’s appointment to senior government positions and the rise of Siniša Mali were important elements of this effort. Through figures such as these, individuals from business, academia, and the NGO sector were brought into the state administration and political leadership to provide the regime with professional legitimacy and an image of modernisation. This alliance remained relatively limited and unstable. Universities, led by the University of Belgrade, never became firm strongholds of the ruling party. University teachers and researchers had long expressed dissatisfaction with the regime, although this dissatisfaction was not necessarily associated with a shared opposition ideology. Shortly before the outbreak of the student protests, the conflict intensified following announcements that foreign private universities might be granted access to public funds intended for higher education. Such a model, resembling certain systems of education vouchers, raised the possibility of diverting budgetary resources from public universities to private institutions. The academic community regarded this as a threat of further subordinating education to business interests connected with political power. The conflict between universities and the regime therefore also concerned the academic community’s immediate material interests. When the canopy of the reconstructed railway station in Novi Sad collapsed in November 2024, killing sixteen people, this existing conflict acquired an entirely new dimension. The tragedy was widely perceived as emblematic of a system in which political loyalty, opaque management, and corrupt relationships displaced expertise and professional responsibility. Regardless of the specific technical causes of the collapse, the question arose of how a major infrastructure project, presented as a symbol of the country’s modernisation, could have been completed without adequate safety oversight. The student rebellion that followed received broad support from university teachers. This alliance also had a very immediate foundation: students and professors already knew one another, encountered each other daily at their faculties, and shared the same institutional space. For students, the academic elite included their own professors, with whom they could communicate and cooperate directly. Despite occasional conflicts over the blockades, universities, particularly the University of Belgrade, became crucial pillars of the movement, providing institutional, moral, and practical support. The regime responded to the rebellion by relying even more heavily on party cadres. The formation of Đuro Macut’s government, following the political crisis caused by the protests, did not bring about any meaningful reconciliation with the academic community. Figures who had failed to demonstrate sufficient party loyalty were further pushed out of government, reinforcing a system in which real political power rested within the informal party hierarchy, while ministers and other formal officeholders enjoyed limited autonomy. Student plenums and the emergence of a populist movement The student movement that emerged from the university blockades developed a distinctive organizational model based on direct democracy. Plenums were established at faculties, where students made decisions about demands, protests, and other activities. Participation in these plenums varied considerably, and informal hierarchies emerged over time. Working groups responsible for preparing proposals often acquired substantial autonomy, while plenums ratified decisions shaped by a relatively small number of active participants. As the movement continued, the number of students directly involved in everyday decision-making gradually declined. Although the organizational model of the plenums had affinities with anarchist and horizontal traditions, their political content was not revolutionary…The radicalism of the student movement lay primarily in its methods of organization and its challenge to the existing government, rather than in its ideological program. Nevertheless, the plenums retained their role as the primary source of the student movement’s legitimacy. Their importance also lay in their ability to generate broad social mobilisation. Student marches between cities, multi-day walks, cycling tours, mass demonstrations, and complex logistical operations involved large numbers of young people. Many did not necessarily participate in formulating political demands, but through organizing these activities they became active members of the movement. The student movement enabled them to become part of a broader political community through collective action, without requiring them to adopt a particular political ideology beforehand. Students carefully avoided ideological and political positions that might undermine broad social support, seeking to present themselves as a movement representing the interests of society as a whole. Although the organizational model of the plenums had affinities with anarchist and horizontal traditions, their political content was not revolutionary. Broad participation encouraged the reproduction of prevailing social attitudes, since only demands acceptable to large numbers Of participants could gain support. The radicalism of the student movement lay primarily in its methods of organization and its challenge to the existing government, rather than in its ideological program. The alliance of populism and expertise The most unusual feature of the student movement was its alliance with the academic elite. In many contemporary Western societies, populist movements develop in opposition to educated elites, experts, and professional managers. Academic institutions are often portrayed as part of an alienated establishment, removed from the everyday concerns of ordinary people. In Serbia, a mass populist movement embraced the academic elite as a natural political ally. Education, expertise, professional qualifications, and cultural capital became central elements of its political identity. This was clearly reflected in how students were presented in public. They were described as educated, decent, responsible, and capable young people: future doctors, engineers, professors, and specialists. Particular emphasis was placed on the message that they wanted to remain in Serbia and build their professional futures in their own country. This narrative corresponded directly to the experience of dissatisfaction with Vučić’s regime. In a society where employment and advancement depend on party connections, the natural alternative appears to be one in which knowledge, qualifications, and professional competence are valued. The struggle against corruption and nepotism thus became the link between the academic elite and the populist base. This alliance also involved a certain fetishisation of expertise: the expectation that people with appropriate education and professional qualifications, free from connections to the compromised political class, would be better equipped to govern the country. Such a belief overlooks the fact that expertise in a particular field does not automatically translate into political competence, and that professional elites have their own social interests, which do not always coincide with those of the majority of the population. Nevertheless, the combination of populist mobilisation and the authority of expertise enabled the student movement to move beyond the universities and become a serious political alternative. This was also reflected in the composition of the Student List. Its candidates included university professors, economists, lawyers, specialists from various fields, and a significant number of people from non-governmental organizations. Why the student movement did not develop a new ideology When the student movement decided to stop directing demands at the existing government and instead call for parliamentary elections, it took a step that might initially have appeared to abandon its original logic of direct democracy. Yet this decision was consistent with the movement’s populist character. Although based on principles of direct democracy, the student plenums reproduced another dominant social belief: that parliamentary elections are the principal mechanism of political change. At the same time, they maintained their distance from existing political parties. This was often explained by the organizational characteristics of the student movement. Since the plenums had no permanent representatives authorised to negotiate on behalf of the movement as a whole, cooperation with political parties was institutionally complicated. There was also a deeper ideological reason. The student movement could not easily negotiate a common program with parties holding clearly defined political positions. Cooperation with liberals, conservatives, nationalists, or social democrats would have required the movement to take positions on questions over which its own base was divided. Its political strength depended on its ability to avoid opening up these divisions. The Student List represented what was widely perceived in society as political normality. Its fundamental demand was for a state free from corruption, institutions that function properly, and expertise to take precedence over party affiliation. The election campaign was therefore largely free of traditional ideological conflicts. Vučić attempted to portray the Student List as a political force that would change his economic and foreign policies, jeopardise relations with Russia, or call existing social benefits into question. The Student List generally responded that such changes were not its objective and that it would implement existing policies more effectively and responsibly. There was considerably more programmatic continuity between the two largest electoral lists than the intensity of their political confrontation might suggest. The Student List represented what was widely perceived in society as political normality. Its fundamental demand was for a state free from corruption, institutions that function properly, and expertise to take precedence over party affiliation…There was considerably more programmatic continuity between the two largest electoral lists than the intensity of their political confrontation might suggest. Even when the Student List expressed opposition to the low-wage labor policy promoted by Vučić’s regime during its early years, the difference was not entirely clear. Over the preceding decade, the regime itself had attempted to move away from the image of a country attracting foreign investors exclusively through low wages, instead promoting technological development, investment in science, and more sophisticated industrial investment. There is a substantial difference between political rhetoric and actual economic outcomes, but the conflict largely concerned who was capable of realising the desired economic model. A similar logic applied to foreign policy. Vučić’s government sought to maintain relations with the European Union, Russia, and China while avoiding complete alignment with any single international bloc. This policy enjoyed relatively broad support in society, giving the Student List little reason to challenge it radically. The central electoral choice was much simpler: the continuation of a system based on party loyalty or its replacement by one promising professional governance. A referendum-like victory and the defeat of the political class The election results confirmed the strength of this political mobilisation. According to preliminary data from the Republic Electoral Commission, the Student List won 52.65 percent of the vote, while the list led by Aleksandar Vučić received 39.22 percent. Turnout was approximately 69 percent, and seat projections indicated that the Student List could form a parliamentary majority on its own. Vučić’s electoral machine managed to retain a substantial part of its voter base, but could not match the exceptionally broad mobilisation of voters seeking political change. The student movement succeeded in giving the election the character of a referendum. Voting was presented as a decision on whether the existing system of government should survive, and this atmosphere effectively eliminated the space for traditional opposition parties. Most withdrew from the electoral race, while those that remained achieved negligible results. No non-minority list other than the two dominant ones crossed the electoral threshold. The student movement thus defeated Vučić and effectively replaced the previous opposition. This may be the most important political consequence of the election. Serbia has not acquired a new governing party representing a clearly defined ideological alternative to the previous government. A movement whose legitimacy rests on the combination of mass mobilisation, rejection of corruption, and trust in expertise has secured a parliamentary majority. Real estate development: the drug fueling Vučić’s economic model Vučić’s regime survived thanks to its electoral machine and clientelist relationships, but its political stability also depended on its ability to deliver economic growth, relative stability in living standards, and increased purchasing power. The previous government’s economic policy was more complex than it is often portrayed in opposition circles. Over the preceding decade, Serbia benefited from certain advantages arising from its foreign policy position. Maintaining relations with Russia provided access to relatively affordable energy, while cooperation with China brought significant investment, particularly in industry, mining, and infrastructure. In this respect, Serbia’s economic model shared certain similarities with the policies pursued by Hungary and Slovakia. At the same time, maintaining a stable Serbian currency exchange rate against the euro was an important instrument for preserving purchasing power. For a population whose consumption depends substantially on imported goods, and for citizens with loans or other obligations denominated in euros, exchange-rate stability had immediate economic significance. The regime also sought to secure increases in pensions, public-sector wages, and various forms of social benefits. Regardless of the actual scope and distributional effects of these measures, they contributed to maintaining social support for the existing economic model. Real estate development became one of its most important pillars. Major infrastructure projects, the development of residential and commercial complexes, the Belgrade Waterfront project, preparations for EXPO, and related urban developments sustained construction activity, created jobs, and contributed to GDP growth. The problem was the economy’s excessive reliance on large, often luxury construction projects, whose contribution to economic activity largely ended when construction was completed. Moreover, a substantial share of the work was carried out by foreign companies that brought in their own workers and departed after completing the projects, leaving limited long-term benefits for the domestic economy. In Serbia, real estate development also had a distinctly political function. Major construction and infrastructure projects were among the key mechanisms linking political and business elites. Control over land, urban planning decisions, public procurement, and investment projects created opportunities for private capital accumulation. Real estate development thus became one of the mechanisms through which individuals connected to political power could themselves become capitalists. This model generated a powerful interdependence between political authority, investors, and the construction sector. Political control provided access to profitable projects, while those projects contributed to the economic growth on which the government based part of its legitimacy. Real estate development thus became one of the mechanisms through which individuals connected to political power could themselves become capitalists. This model generated a powerful interdependence between political authority, investors, and the construction sector. In this sense, real estate development became a kind of drug for Vučić’s regime. It made it possible to satisfy two important demands simultaneously: continued enrichment of the politically connected business elite and the maintenance of sufficiently high levels of economic activity for living standards to rise. Every new major project prolonged the operation of this model while increasing dependence on its continued expansion. The future of major urban development projects therefore became politically significant. The Student List’s opposition to plans for the commercial redevelopment of the General Staff complex in Belgrade, linked to the investment interests of the family of U.S. President Donald Trump, was one visible expression of the rejection of the previous approach to managing urban space and public resources. The new government will consequently face a serious problem: if it intends to dismantle the corrupt mechanisms of the previous regime, it will also have to change the way one of the economy’s important engines of growth operates. The economic constraints facing the new government The Student List presented an ambitious reform program, particularly in education, science, culture, healthcare, and social protection. This program reflects its social composition and the significant role of the academic and professional elite in shaping it. Fulfilling these promises will require substantial public resources. One assumption underlying the new government’s optimism is that combating corruption will free up sufficient resources to finance the promised reforms. More transparent public procurement, more rational investment, and reduced misuse of public funds could certainly produce substantial savings. The question remains, however, whether they will be sufficient. Even with a significant reduction in corruption, Serbia would continue to face low productivity, limited public revenues, dependence on foreign investment, and structural weaknesses in its domestic economy. The potential redirection of economic development presents a particularly complex challenge. If the new government sought to reduce dependence on real estate development and place greater emphasis on export-oriented production, it would encounter constraints arising from the existing monetary and economic model. Strengthening the competitiveness of domestic agriculture and certain industrial sectors, for example, could raise questions about the real value of the dinar. Depreciation of the domestic currency might improve the price competitiveness of exports, but it would also make imported goods more expensive and undermine purchasing power. Such a move would not automatically solve problems in production and could have serious social consequences. Preserving purchasing power was one of the Student List’s important promises. Its populist base does not expect an economic policy that asks citizens to accept declining living standards in the name of long-term development goals. Similar constraints apply to the emigration of young and educated people. Over the previous two years, the student movement strongly emphasised that young people wanted to remain in Serbia and build their futures there. Yet the emigration of educated workers is not exclusively a consequence of corruption or authoritarian government. Croatia’s experience demonstrates that even EU member states can face large-scale labor emigration, while freedom of movement within the European labor market can make migration to wealthier countries easier. The new government will therefore face a range of problems for which there are no simple technical solutions. Its response to the question of future economic development centers primarily on increasing productivity, one of the most difficult tasks of economic policy, requiring long-term structural change rather than merely replacing political personnel. Will the populist base control the new elite? The most important question following the electoral victory concerns the relationship the new government will establish with the movement that brought it to power. Over the previous two years, student plenums had been the primary source of the movement’s legitimacy. They decided on political demands, forms of mobilisation, and ultimately the move into parliamentary politics. The process of compiling the Student List further demonstrated the movement’s insistence on controlling its representatives. Candidates underwent lengthy procedures to scrutinise their biographies and professional integrity, with the aim of preventing the nomination of individuals whose past could compromise the entire movement. This approach reflected the fundamental political message that power should be entrusted to competent and uncompromised individuals. The entry of approximately 140 Student List representatives into parliament creates an entirely new situation. MPs will now possess formal political legitimacy, access to state institutions, and the ability to participate directly in decision-making. They will no longer be merely delegates of a protest movement, but holders of parliamentary mandates. The question is whether the new government will continue to recognise the authority of student plenums and other participatory forms of organization. The plenums themselves have already weakened considerably: their activity is declining, and fewer students are participating. If they manage to preserve their organizational structures and connections with elected representatives, they could function as a mechanism of social control over the new government, limiting the autonomy of professional administrators and their ability to pursue policies contrary to the expectations of the movement’s electoral base. There is also the possibility that the connection with the student movement will gradually be severed. In that case, the academic elite, which already occupies a prominent position within the Student List, could become the dominant political force in the new government. Its representatives might begin to behave like professional political and managerial elites in Western societies, justifying unpopular measures through appeals to economic necessity, fiscal responsibility, or market demands. The Student List’s MPs hold a range of political convictions. Some are closer to liberal and pro- European positions, others to conservative or nationalist ones, while some candidates are associated with socially oriented policies. As long as the main objective was to remove Vučić’s regime, these differences did not have to become politically decisive. Once the new government faces concrete questions of taxation, privatisation, public spending, labor legislation, and international relations, ideological conflicts may become unavoidable. It is easy to imagine liberal, conservative, nationalist, or left-wing groupings gradually emerging within the parliamentary majority. Such a development would mark the end of the distinctive populist unity that made electoral victory possible and could open the way to neoliberal reforms, austerity policies, or other measures that directly threaten the living standards of sections of the population. The Student List’s MPs hold a range of political convictions…It is easy to imagine liberal, conservative, nationalist, or left-wing groupings gradually emerging within the parliamentary majority. Such a development would mark the end of the distinctive populist unity that made electoral victory possible and could open the way to neoliberal reforms, austerity policies, or other measures that directly threaten the living standards of sections of the population. Between political normalisation and a new democracy The Student List’s victory demonstrated that even an exceptionally sophisticated party machine can be defeated through broad social mobilisation. The student movement united a large part of the population around demands to end corruption, nepotism, and party control over institutions. Its fundamental promise was one of political normalisation. The immediate consequences of this victory are already visible. From the perspective of Radnički glas (Workers’ Voice), an organization of which I am a member and which works with trade unions in education, research, culture, and other sectors, the change in political relations was felt practically overnight. Just one day after the election, we are already observing changes in the behavior of certain directors and managers, while questions are emerging about the future of numerous proceedings initiated against employees who opposed the government. A military trade union that announced several months ago that it was ceasing its activities because of political pressure has now issued a new statement, suggesting that it may resume its work. Party nepotism was an everyday experience for large numbers of employees. For many people, the Student List’s victory therefore brings a sense of liberation from immediate pressure. The possibility of speaking more freely at work, refusing a political instruction, or planning a professional future without dependence on party loyalty represents a tangible change. This helps explain the mass celebrations following the election. The victory has also opened up the possibility of transforming political representation itself. Here we encounter perhaps the most interesting, and seemingly paradoxical, similarity between the Student List and Vučić’s regime. Both, in different ways, displaced the traditional multiparty system based on competition between ideologically defined parties. Vučić incorporated different political options into his governing coalition, subordinating them to the party apparatus and its hierarchy. The Student List brought together ideologically diverse representatives around a common political objective, but built their legitimacy through mass participation rather than a traditional party organization. The absence of clearly defined party programs need not be a weakness of the new political order. Competition between political parties, in which citizens periodically choose between pre- formulated programs, is not the only possible form of democratic representation. The student movement demonstrated that enormous numbers of people who had never belonged to political parties or previously engaged in political activism could be mobilised. Their participation extended beyond protests to organizing the election campaign, protecting polling stations, and directly monitoring the electoral process. People who had previously been merely voters became active participants in political life. The question is whether this form of participation can be sustained after the electoral victory. Student plenums have already weakened, but the social energy released by the movement need not remain tied exclusively to them. It is particularly significant that many Student List candidates are professionally established individuals with no previous political ambitions. Their willingness to accept parliamentary mandates does not necessarily imply a desire to become professional politicians. Understanding political office as a temporary social responsibility could help establish a different relationship between representatives and those they represent. Trade unions could play an important role in this process. Unlike student plenums, whose activity is linked to the changing composition of the student population, trade unions have more durable organizational structures, direct connections with employees, and concrete demands arising from everyday employment relations. In the political space opening up after the fall of the previous regime, they could establish themselves as one of the organized voices from below. This would also entail a different relationship with parliamentary power. Trade unions would not have to confine themselves to traditional social dialogue, appeals to ministries, and occasional negotiations with government officials. They could establish lasting connections with Student List MPs, following the example of the cooperation they developed with student plenums during the protests, and use these relationships to articulate workers’ demands and exert pressure on the government. Implementing the promises made in the student program, including the expansion of labor rights, could provide a common framework for such action, while unions preserve their independence and their role as the organized voice of workers. Such a relationship could offer a way beyond the limitations of representative parliamentary democracy. Organized social groups could participate directly in shaping political decisions and overseeing their implementation. Parliament could then become a place where the demands of the social base are articulated, rather than an institution in which professional politicians make decisions independently between electoral cycles. The most important possibility opened up by the Student List’s victory lies in the opportunity to free political representation from its exclusive dependence on party competition and to build a more lasting connection between elected representatives and an active, organized society. The student movement has already demonstrated that mass political participation can exist outside traditional political parties. Its next challenge will be to show whether that participation can endure when representatives of the movement constitute the governing parliamentary majority. articles.title: Fossil Fuels Are “Undermining Democracy” & Must Be Phased Out: Climate Activist Kumi Naidoo at COP31
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. There are just four days remaining for nearly 200 countries to come to some agreement on the next steps to tackle climate change. On Monday, negotiators published a wide-ranging 18-page draft document that’s been characterized as a shopping list of language and issues to be debated ahead of a Friday deadline for a final agreement. This is the global policy lead for Oil Change International. ROMAIN IOUALALEN : So, I think this is a text that was designed to basically please everyone, and they took, you know, the best, the most ambitious demands from each group and put it in there. Obviously, throughout this week, what we’re going to see is a game of massacre in the negotiations. We’re going to see a lot of these — a lot of these recommendations or this language going to be cut by parties that don’t agree with any of this. And so, as the president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, just said, the text that we’re going to end up with is going to look very different. AMY GOODMAN : Agreements here at COP are made by consensus, meaning every country essentially has veto power over the final text. Rich countries and fossil fuel-producing countries have historically thwarted the most ambitious climate goals. These negotiations, of course, are happening as the Iran war has also drawn global attention to the world’s dependence on fossil fuels. So, what will it take to bring an end to the fossil fuel era? A bloc of nearly 30 countries from the Global South have started a parallel process that’s aiming for a binding agreement to transition away from fossil fuels — a fossil fuel treaty. The first official conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels was held in Santa Marta, Colombia, earlier this year. Nearly 60 countries attended. A follow-up conference is scheduled to take place next year in Tuvalu. To talk more about what can be achieved at this U.N. climate summit and what makes the process that began in Santa Marta different, we’re joined here in Turkey by Kumi Naidoo, longtime climate justice activist from South Africa, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. It’s nice to have you back, to see you again, Kumi. Let’s talk about what’s happened so far at this climate summit. In a moment, we’re going to be talking to the former ambassador from Nepal. They just suffered a calamitous glacier melting that led to at least 7,000 people dead and missing. That’s just one example of thousands. What has to happen here? And what is happening? KUMI NAIDOO : We need to get serious about addressing the root cause of climate change. Eighty-six percent of what’s driving the crisis is our addiction and dependency on oil, coal and gas, what we call fossil fuels. The difficulty we have is that for 30 years of negotiations, we don’t have any mention of fossil fuels. That’s like Alcoholics Anonymous holding 30 years of conferences and not mentioning alcohol in the outcome document. Now, there are important things that we are pushing here on to get clarity on what a just transition would look like, trying to get resources to go in the Loss and Damage Fund and so on. But what is patently clear right now is we need a parallel process, one that will lead us to a binding agreement. So, what we’ve achieved in April through the Santa Marta conference is a parallel process that’s linked to the COP , right? And that is one way we hope we can grow the number of countries that are serious about fossil fuel phaseout. The good thing is the momentum is there. We are not seeing here, still, enough movement on finance. Because let’s be very clear: You cannot tell poor countries in the Global South, who are carrying a lot of debt to the Global North, that they must stop producing fossil fuels, when rich countries continue to expand their fossil fuel production. The important thing is, any new, fresh investment, knowing what we know, knowing that every region, just not Nepal — every region in the world this year has experienced loss of life, serious events and so on. So we don’t even need the science anymore to tell us that we are in a deep crisis. And so far, I have to say, we are not seeing the urgency here, either on providing finance or on addressing the need to start phasing out fossil fuels. AMY GOODMAN : It’s the largest U.N. climate summit here, I mean, something like 90,000 people. What’s the percentage of fossil fuel lobbyists and fossil fuel representatives in different governments? But also, there are many, many people deeply committed to dealing with climate change. Explain how it all happens and the terms that are like another language to the rest of the world, when you say, I mean, even “climate justice,” what that means. But here, it’s “climate finance.” It’s words like “ambition.” What do these mean? KUMI NAIDOO : OK, on ambition, the science has told us that we have to keep warming below 1.5 degrees. We are already pushing towards that. That means from the time that we started burning fossil fuels, we cannot have a collective temperature rise beyond that. So, ambition means we need to take the actions to keep us within that threshold. In terms of finance, what we are saying is that if we are saying to poor countries, “Leave the oil in the ground. Leave the coal in the ground. Leave the gas underneath the ground,” then they are willing to do that. But they’re saying, “Well, you built your economies in the rich countries on the basis of exploiting all those resources. So, you help us now to actually finance the new energies transition.” And let’s be very clear: Today, Donald Trump actually has become the accidental advocate for the phaseout of fossil fuels. The U.S.-Iran illegal, unjustified war — and let’s be very blunt: There was no nuclear weapons. His own national intelligence adviser said there wasn’t and resigned. This is a war which we in the Global South call the Epstein war. This was a distraction from other crises that he had. But what it’s done is that so many countries, rich and poor countries, have said we have to now move to actually start building renewable energies. And we’re seeing a scale-up, because, clearly, it doesn’t make sense for us to continue to do that. The one important point is, we have to recognize that fossil fuels is not only bad for the climate. Fossil fuels has been the major driver of war and conflict. The Harvard study says 7 million people are dying yearly now from carbon pollution, so it’s a negative health impact. And as we’ve seen in the United States when Trump convened the CEOs of the fossil fuel companies before the elections, we are seeing that the fossil fuel companies everywhere around the world are actually undermining democracy. So, basically, the fight to restrict the power of the fossil fuel industry and put them out of business as fast as possible — we’re not thinking it will be done overnight, but we have to do it on the fastest possible timeline, in a fair way, and in which we are able to support and fund those countries who are saying, “Don’t exploit it for short-term profit, for long-term disaster. And stop playing political poker with the future of our children and the future of our planet.” AMY GOODMAN : Explain Santa Marta. What happened in Colombia? What is the fossil fuel treaty? KUMI NAIDOO : So, firstly, the fossil fuel treaty does not exist. It’s a Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, right? You remember, Amy, in Copenhagen, what we were asking for: a FAB deal — not a fabulous deal, a “fair, ambitious and binding” deal. AMY GOODMAN : This was 2009. KUMI NAIDOO : '09, right? And the binding deal has never happened. And so, what we are saying is that unless we can move in the direction, like on nuclear weapons, where we moved to a Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty — not perfect. The rich countries still, you know, ignore it, as we know. If we don't have something equivalent — so, in Santa Marta, we got about 57 countries coming together saying, “We are serious about phasing out fossil fuel,” because here, there isn’t a conversation about fossil fuel phaseout, even though it’s 86%. It’s ridiculous, right? And so, what Santa Marta has given us is a parallel and connected process to the COP where we are focusing on what would it take to actually do the phaseout on the fastest possible timeline. AMY GOODMAN : The right-wing president of Colombia has pulled Colombia out of the Santa Marta treaty initiative, which was accomplished under former president — KUMI NAIDOO : President Petro. AMY GOODMAN : — ironically, his name, Petro. KUMI NAIDOO : Yeah. Listen, one country making a move is not going to be the end of the process. The important thing is, people forget, it’s not just the 57 countries that went to Santa Marta, though that gave momentum to the U.N. General Assembly having a vote a few weeks later, where the International Court of Justice advisory opinion said countries needed to phase out fossil fuels and governments had a moral and legal responsibility to attack. A hundred and forty-one countries voted to support that, and by the way, the 11 countries that voted against it included Iran and the U.S. They might be bombing the hell out of each other, but they’re united on fossil fuels. AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to go back to another issue. In May of 2024, Turkey announced a total trade embargo on Israel. In his opening speech, the Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan described the suffering of the Palestinian people as, quote, “not only genocide, but also ecocide,” and called for a shift from “empty dialogue to direct implementation,” unquote. But a new report has revealed that despite Turkey’s declared trade embargo on Israel, at least 77 shipments of crude oil from the Turkish port of Ceyhan were delivered to Ashkelon in Israel as of June of this year. We were just at the People’s Climate Summit today, which is also taking place in another part of Antalya. You’ve also spoken there. A group of Turkish and global civil society activists demanded a stop to Turkish oil transfers to Israel. I had a chance to speak on Sunday with Joseph Griso from Energy Embargo for Palestine. Their new report, “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.” JOSEPH GRISO : My name is Joseph. I’m here as a representative of Energy Embargo for Palestine. And ourselves, along with the Palestinian Youth Movement and the Progressive International, have produced this landmark report, which really clearly details the role that Türkiye is playing, specifically the port of Ceyhan in the south of Turkey is playing, in secretly delivering crude oil to the state of Israel. AMY GOODMAN : So, the report is called “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.” JOSEPH GRISO : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : Explain what you have found out. JOSEPH GRISO : So, there is a key oil infrastructure pipeline, the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, the BTC pipeline, and that is responsible for over 40% of the crude oil that Israel receives. This is crude oil that is, of course, refined in Israel and converted into oil products that are capable of — that play a key, integral role in sustaining the the military operations that have been responsible for the genocide in Gaza. AMY GOODMAN : And how did you get the information? JOSEPH GRISO : So, in May 2024, Türkiye announced its trade embargo. But what we were seeing through our analysis of shipping data, as well as our analysis of satellite images, is that the oil trade, very specifically transfers of oil from Ceyhan to Ashkelon port in Israel, have continued. And our report clearly details 77 specific oil shipments that have continued since May 2024 up to June 2026 to show that this is a constant, this is a secret and systematic trade pattern that is continuing to uphold Israel’s ability to carry out the genocide. And so, we’re calling for the Turkish government to halt these oil supplies, this oil route. And we’re calling really specifically for them to look at the two Greek shipping companies which are responsible, along with BP and SOCAR , the owners of the pipeline, to stop this oil trade and to implement sanctions, as well as legal processes, to uphold their trade embargo. AMY GOODMAN : So, that’s Joseph Griso from Energy Embargo for Palestine. Their new report , “Exposing Türkiye’s Secret Crude Oil Shipments to Israel.” And before we end, Kumi Naidoo, since you are from South Africa and South Africa has brought Israel to the International Court of Justice around the issue of genocide and war crimes, your thoughts on what they’re talking about? And this also goes to the issue of fossil fuels fueling war and violence. KUMI NAIDOO : I’d just like to remind people about what Nelson Mandela said. He told us, as South Africans, we will never be free until the Palestinian people are free. And that action that was brought at the International Court of Justice, which has said that probably there’s a genocide — but let’s be very clear: Amnesty, including the two main human rights organizations within Israel, have declared it a genocide. You know, most of the American people can see it’s genocide, and that, we understand, played a role in the midterm elections. And to President Erdoğan, I would make an appeal to him: Please be consistent. You say the right things on Palestine, but to continue to fuel the genocide by giving them war takes away the legitimacy of what you are saying. But more so, we have to say to President Erdoğan, as well, that you must release the political prisoners, who are in the thousands in Turkish prisons. They include politicians. They include writers, journalists and so on. And it’s also important that we note that just as this happens, on the eve of it, the LGBTI community has been attacked on a massive basis here. And what we need to understand is the climate justice issue and social justice issues are absolutely connected. And as a South African and somebody who fought for human rights, we feel that right now the United States, under President Trump, is not only undermining the climate agenda; they are setting back us on democracy. They’re setting back us on human rights. And actually, today, the United States, under Trump, has become, without any doubt, a net negative source in the world. And we hope that the American people, who are rising up through the midterms and so on, continue to stand in partnership. The important thing, I would say, is, which you mentioned, three states in the U.S., their legislatures have passed formal resolutions endorsing the idea of a fossil fuel treaty: California, Hawaii and Maine. And in addition to that, about 40 United States cities, from Philadelphia to San Francisco to Pittsburgh, have all endorsed it. So, the people of the U.S. are saying they want to be part of the global effort to phase out fossil fuels, to get a binding agreement. And what we would say to the American people, your brothers and sisters around the world are ready to embrace you, and we do not see American people as what the Trump administration represents to the world today. AMY GOODMAN : And we are going to talk about the U.S. in just one minute, but I wanted to extend our condolences on the death of Desmond D’Sa, the South African anti-pollution campaigner who died in a car accident. KUMI NAIDOO : Desmond D’Sa was an inspiration to all of us. I was at his funeral and memorial service. And Bobby Peek, who you might also have known, here, who worked with him. It’s a devastation. But what’s so beautiful about his life is that he was a working-class person. He got the biggest Goldman Prize of Environment. He never changed. He lived a working-class life, lived close to the people. And what I saw in the U.S. midterm elections, I saw many Desmond D’Sas emerge. And I hope that the mainstream of the Democratic Party will allow those voices to actually become more prominent, because the world needs those kinds of voices in the leadership of the United States. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s not forget Desmond D’Sa’s last name is spelled D-S-A. Kumi Naidoo, longtime human rights and climate justice activist from South Africa, president of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. Coming up, while the Trump administration has pulled out of the U.N. climate summit, a number of U.S. mayors and governors came here. Many more are pledging to address the climate crisis at the state and local level. California Governor Gavin Newsom was one who came here and said he’s 100% behind a fossil fuel phaseout. We’ll speak with journalist Mark Hertsgaard. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Mirvari Dance Ensemble performing “Holiday Suite” during the Climate Week summit in September.

articles.title: As U.S. Boycotts U.N. Climate Talks, California Leads State/City Efforts to Combat Climate Crisis
articles.content: For the second year in a row, the Trump administration has not sent an official delegation to the United Nations’ annual climate change conference, held this year in Antalya, Turkey. But although no federal representatives are present, more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders are participating, including the governor of the fourth-largest economy in the world, California Governor Gavin Newsom. Newsom, a likely candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, has endorsed the Santa Marta Process, a coalition of nations working to develop a global green energy transition. “The petrostates have made it abundantly clear: Under the current rules of consensus, they are never, ever going to allow COPs to succeed. They’re just not going to sign that agreement. So, essentially, the Santa Marta coalition is making an end run around that, using economic power,” says longtime environmental and climate reporter Mark Hertsgaard.

articles.title: Bangladesh Faces Mounting Climate Crisis While Wealthy, Polluting Nations Resist Calls to Pay Up
articles.content: Bangladesh’s first riverkeeper, Sharif Jamil, shares how poor countries in the Global South are struggling to effectively adapt to climate change as rising sea levels, extreme weather patterns, pollution and more are creating an escalating “humanitarian catastrophe,” while the wealthy impede efforts to reallocate financial resources for adaptation and mitigation. “If you want to protect the planet, if you want to save the planet from global warming, you need climate finance to make all this transition,” says Jamil.

articles.title: Senegal shipwreck adds to hundreds of migrant deaths at sea
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The death toll from a migrant shipwreck off northwestern Senegal has risen to 43 , as search teams recovered more bodies along the coast near Loumpoul, between Dakar and Saint-Louis. Most of the dead were young people from nearby communities. It is the latest in a series of boat disasters that have killed more than 200 migrants on major migration routes over the past three months, as people trying to reach Europe and other destinations by sea continue to face deadly risks. On November 9, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported that at least 56 people had died in a series of shipwrecks off Senegal and Greece over the weekend. The Senegal disaster occurred on the Western African Atlantic route, now one of the main corridors for migrants. Also, according to IOM, at least 454 people died or went missing on this route in 2026 as of October 26. The organization says these are minimum estimates, because many boats disappear without survivors or trace. The economic conditions driving migration Despite the risks associated with the journey, migration along the route continues. Economic hardship is one of the major factors driving migration from Africa towards Europe and the Gulf. High unemployment, low wages, rising food and housing costs, and limited job opportunities have made it increasingly difficult for many people, particularly young people, to sustain themselves and their families. In countries where agriculture remains a major source of livelihood, drought, declining agricultural productivity, land dispossession, and limited access to markets have further weakened household incomes. Senegal’s national statistics agency put unemployment among economically active citizens between the ages of 15 to 34 at 23.5% in the second quarter of 2026. An estimated 35.3% of all 15–24-year-olds were neither employed nor in education or training, rising to 46.3% in rural areas. These conditions are also within wider economic inequalities between Africa and wealthier regions of the world. While African countries continue to supply raw materials, agricultural products, and labor to international markets, the benefits of this economic activity are often unevenly distributed. Debt repayments, austerity measures, privatization, and limited public investment have also constrained governments’ capacity to expand employment and provide essential services. Many people leave not simply because they want to live abroad, but because they cannot find decent work or secure a sustainable livelihood at home. Restricting their movement does little to resolve the conditions driving migration. Fewer arrivals, more deaths Data published by the IOM on September 17 showed that nearly 60,000 migrants and refugees had reached Europe by sea as of September 15, a 39% decline from the 98,040 recorded during the same period in 2025. However, at least 2,292 people had died or gone missing attempting these crossings, compared with 1,999 during the corresponding period in 2025. The Central Mediterranean route to Italy recorded the sharpest decline in arrivals, falling by 55%, from 48,231 to 21,393. At the same time, deaths and disappearances along the route increased from 844 to 996. On the Eastern Mediterranean route, deaths and disappearances also rose, from 284 to 417, despite fewer arrivals in Greece. These figures reveal the limitations of measuring the success of migration policies primarily through declining arrivals. While European governments may present fewer arrivals as evidence of effective border enforcement, the rising number of deaths and disappearances shows that the dangers of maritime migration have not disappeared. Instead, these measures have reshaped migration routes and patterns of movement pushing more people towards smuggling networks and dangerous sea crossings, particularly in areas where search-and-rescue operations are inadequate. Ultimately, without addressing the root causes of why people migrate, people will continue to take whatever physical risks they need to take if it means the possibility of economic survival.

articles.title: Gen Z protests in Germany met with racial profiling and police harassment
articles.author: Leon Wystrychowski
articles.content: Even before the protests, held under the slogan “Gen Z Takes Charge” (“Gen Z regelt“), took place, politicians and mainstream media had been spreading scenarios of impending chaos. Around 120,000 people, mostly teenagers and young adults, took to the streets in more than 30 German cities to protest cuts to social welfare and compulsory military service, and to demand climate protection. Citing the mass protests in neighboring France – which, as usual, are portrayed in Germany’s dominant public discourse primarily as vandalism and rioting – the authorities and media also predicted a wave of violence for October 31, the day of the “Gen Z Takes Charge” demonstrations. Although this wave failed to materialize, clashes with the police did occur in several cities. Eyewitnesses report that, as a rule, it was the forces of the state that initiated the escalation. In Frankfurt, a major city, there was also some looting at a shopping mall following the protests, albeit on a limited scale. Whether, as in France, state agent provocateurs were directly involved is another question. In any case, those in power had deliberately whipped up expectations of precisely such incidents. And afterward, they were – predictably – made the centerpiece of media coverage and portrayed in exaggerated terms. “Migrant Milieu” under collective suspicion The “culprits” were quickly identified: Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative CDU/CSU, spoke of perpetrators from “the migrant milieu.” He received backing for this statement from fellow party members and the far-right AfD, as well as from conservative mainstream media. Words were quickly followed by action. In Frankfurt, the police have since launched a large-scale racial profiling campaign in the area surrounding the mall where the disturbances took place on October 31. After one week, the police proudly announced that they had carried out more than 1,000 checks. Those affected, however, are exclusively children, teenagers, and young adults – male and female – with dark skin and dark hair. Police officers arbitrarily stop these people as they walk around downtown, go shopping, eat, drink, or simply sit around with friends or family, or on their own, talking or making phone calls. They are ordered to show their IDs and open their bags. Police officers frequently even demand to search their victims’ cell phones. Young men standing side by side in a row against a wall, like dangerous hardened criminals caught red-handed, surrounded and cordoned off by several rows of police officers who also keep eyewitnesses at a distance, have now become an everyday sight in downtown Frankfurt. Racial profiling is officially prohibited in Germany. The term the police use to justify their actions is “checks without reasonable suspicion.” The fact that everyone affected belongs to the group Interior Minister Dobrindt has labeled “the migrant milieu,” and that the same individuals are sometimes stopped and searched two or even three times within a short period, is supposedly all just a coincidence. When asked about the racist checks, a Frankfurt police spokesperson cynically explained that the reason so many people of color were being stopped was that Frankfurt was “such a wonderfully diverse city.” Apparently, some of the spokesperson’s colleagues had not yet gotten the wording down. Deniz Avan, a left-wing local politician, told the left-wing daily junge Welt that a police officer he had confronted let something slip, inadvertently starting to say “Mi-” before cutting himself short and saying something about the “Gen Z” protests instead. Manufacturing a new enemy: “Islamo-Marxism” The campaign must be viewed in the context of militarization, the drive toward war against Russia, the associated policies of dismantling social protections and democratic rights, and the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany. Sharif Wali, an antifascist activist from Frankfurt, told BreakThrough News that there are three reasons behind the current racist campaign: young people who are currently becoming politicized are meant to be intimidated; racism directed against migrants and refugees is meant to be further stoked; and “the police state in Germany is meant to be further advanced.” The fact that the aim is to undermine political protest and resistance by marginalized groups is also evident in the way racism is being combined with an unmistakably anti-left agenda. Even before the “Gen Z Takes Charge” protests, Alexander Throm, the CDU/CSU’s spokesperson on domestic affairs in the German Bundestag, had warned of an “unholy alliance between left-wing extremist forces, sections of the migrant milieu, and criminals.” Immediately after the incidents in Frankfurt, Dobrindt had also blamed “left-wing groups and troublemakers from the migrant milieu,” before subsequently focusing on the latter. In doing so, the two leading conservative politicians are picking up a narrative that has been circulating among right-wing circles for some time and that recently entered the German mainstream following the Left Party’s election victory in the capital, Berlin : an alliance between “left-wing extremists” and “criminal migrants” – or, alternatively, “Islamists.” In France, right-wing politicians have been warning against “Islamo-Gauchisme” for several years. By now, this narrative has crossed over into Germany under the label “Islamo-Marxism.” The parallel with the Nazis’ notion of “Jewish Bolshevism” is obvious. It is equally clear that this modified image of the enemy fits all too neatly with the current political course pursued by those in power in Germany.
